messages.subject: Re: abundance effects in DISTANCE
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 26 Apr 2005 13:33:38 -0400, Richard Chandler wrote:

> >I'm wondering if there are plans to modify DISTANCE so that it can be
> >used to model abundance effects (in addition to detectability effects)
> >in the way described by Royle et al. Ecology 2004 85:1591 and,
> >apparently, Hedley and Buckland 2004? Thanks.

Hi Richard, list,

We are planning to extend Distance to include a new analysis engine based on
the count method of Hedley et al. (2004 - Chapter 4 of the Advanced Distance
Sampling book).  This should hopefully be available by the end of 2005,
funding and time permitting.

In the longer term, we have a research project funded by the US Office of
Naval Research to further extend these methods to deal with problems cased by
(i) local clustering in density that cannot be accommodated by large-scale
smooths; (ii) extrapolating smooth surfaces into areas with no survey effort;
(iii) irregular topography.  This project is due to be completed in June 2007.

 - Len

messages.subject: statistical validity of model selection process?
messages.subject_clean: statistical validity of model selection process?
messages.body_plain:
I just had an interesting talk with my statistician about the whole
validity of modeling detection functions and model selection.  My original
question was about using SAS for bootstrapping ANOVA of  DISTANCE density
estimates for point-count samples of birds in 3 strata.  He told me to junk
the DISTANCE estimates because the results were biased by the model
selection process and the fact that different models by strata mean that
the "measurement tool" (model) is confounded by treatment.  Also, the AIC
model selection process is no better than other numerous model selection
processes, so the selected model is inherently subjective, of unknown
validity, & biased by the particular model selection process used.  He
cited the US Census Bureau as the largest collection of practicing
statisticians, "the mainstream of statistical thought" on this issue, who
decided against using any model-based process for estimating population
size as inherently biased and unreliable.  He suggested I simply truncate
all my data to the distance were the p of detection = 1 for all species and
strata, which post hoc means tossing a lot of data.  He is unconvinced by
my arguments about modeling detection functions and model selection learned
from the wildlife literature and attending several workshops on
mark-recapture modeling and AIC model selection with Anderson, Burnham, or
White.   He was concerned not so much with my particular implementation of
DISTANCE, but with the validity of the whole process, which he considered
an "outlier" (to put it nicely) among the statistical field.  I was a bit
stunned - any comments from the statisticians on the list?

************************
John F. Lehmkuhl
Research Wildlife Biologist
US Forest Service
PNW Research Station
1133 N. Western Ave.
Wenatchee WA 98801
509 664-1737
509 665-8362 fax

messages.subject: Re: statistical validity of model selection process?
messages.subject_clean: statistical validity of model selection process?
messages.body_plain:
John-

There is a lot in your email and I'll try to address some of the
concerns, but my bottom line advice would be to find someone else to
consult with or suggest that he/she run all the additional point counts
needed to collect sufficient data to be able to do the truncation that
they recommend.

Beyond that, if the person stopped to consider what they were
recommending they would realize that choosing a truncation point is a
data-based model and to be objective it would need some type of
criterion (model) to choose the truncation point which can be viewed as
a uniform smooth of the data with an appropriately chosen width such
that the data fit a uniform distribution. It would be a kernel smoother
with a uniform kernel and the parameter is the window width. The
approach he/she is suggesting has been around for 60 years in the ad-hoc
sense (see Kelker estimator).  You can do that if you want.  If you have
sufficient data and your data collection protocol was adequate (ie
little measurement error/rounding), the estimate will be little changed
by the choice of detection functions/models. If you are having to fit
different detection functions for your strata then you would most likely
have to choose different truncation widths unless you chose the minimum
one.  Again, maybe they should be collecting the data.  If they are
suggesting you just choose a truncation width from thin air in which you
"believe" detection is constant, then I'd really question their "wisdom".

With regard to the comment about distance sampling being an "outlier" in
the statitical field, then he/she must also be including the entire
field of statistical probability density estimation (Silverman and
others).  The modelling approach in Distance is simply one way to
provide an estimated probability density function of the observed data.

With regard to the comment about the Census Bureau all I can say is wow!
  Quite a generalization based on a completely different application.  I
can't say I know a lot about the Census Bureau and what you mean by
model-based process but I'd think that most model-based estimators of
abundance that would be applicable to the Census Bureau would be based
on mark-recapture and it is well-known that m-r is susceptible to bias
due to unmodelled heterogeneity.  Distance sampling works on different
principles.  Put another way, the statistician is saying that it is not
possible to estimate a probability density function at a point (namely 0
distance) without a degree of bias that would make it useless. That's
all that distance sampling is. They may want to revisit their comment
after re-considering that but then again ...  If they can't provide a
constructive alternative, I don't listen to people who simply like to
rail.

regards --jeff laake

messages.subject: Re: statistical validity of model selection process?
messages.subject_clean: statistical validity of model selection process?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
Adding to what Jeff has said:

On Tue, 3 May 2005, John F Lehmkuhl wrote:

> > I just had an interesting talk with my statistician about the whole
> > validity of modeling detection functions and model selection.

[..]

> > He cited the US Census Bureau as the largest collection of practicing
> > statisticians, "the mainstream of statistical thought" on this issue,
> > who decided against using any model-based process for estimating
> > population size as inherently biased and unreliable.

As Jeff says, the US Census Bureau are working with very different
applications.  I wonder whether the comment about "model-based process"
is an issue of design-based inference versus model-based.  Working in the
design-based framework is generally to be encouraged in this sort of
application, because it is difficult to justify a single model that is
acceptable to all parties.

The choice of framework (design or model)  affects the choice of
estimators, especially variance estimators.  The book by Thompson
(Sampling, 2002; 2nd Ed) has a very nice discussion of design versus model
issues in Chapter 10.  For example, if our estimators relied on the
assumption that animals should be uniformly distributed across the whole
region, that's an example of an indefensible model that may lead to poor
results. The design-based framework doesn't make any assumptions about the
distribution of animals: variance is due to the sampling process.

However, in distance sampling it is impossible to rely entirely on the
design framework, because we have a fundamental source of non-sampling
error, namely imperfect detection.  There is no way round this except to
use a model.  Our basic inferential framework can be design-based, but we
have to slot in a model at the detectability stage.

Thompson (page 108) says, "Sources of nonsampling error must be modelled
if they are to be taken into account.  Problems of .. detectability must
be modelled in some way in order to adjust for biases and to assess the
uncertainty of estimates."

As Jeff says, there are models and models.  Modelling the detection
function is essentially fitting a density curve to data, and is pretty
uncontroversial in the scheme of things.  The models to avoid are those
that make strong assumptions about the distribution of animals over a wide
area.  In distance sampling we confine assumptions about the distribution
of animals to the narrow search-strips only.

Rachel Fewster

--

messages.body_plain:
Workshop: Counting Critters - An Introduction to Estimating Animal Abundance
and Distance Sampling
16-21 October 2005, Disney s Animal Kingdom, Orlando, Florida, USA
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/counting.critters/

This five-day workshop will introduce participants to the most important
methods of estimating animal abundance in a rigorous but accessible way. In
the first half of the workshop, we cover plot sampling, distance sampling,
mark-recapture and removal methods.  We explain the common key statistical
concepts underlying the methods, use custom-written simulation software to
understand how the methods work, and discuss which method to use when.  In the
second half, we focus on distance sampling in more detail. We discus practical
issues such as use of the software Distance, field methods and survey design.

The workshop is aimed at anyone who needs to estimate wildlife density or
abundance, and is taught by leading researchers from the Centre for Research
into Ecological and Environmental Modelling at the University of St Andrews,
Scotland.

Registration for this workshop is now open.  Since all of our previous
workshops in the USA have been oversubscribed, we encourage everyone
interested to register as soon as possible.

For more details, please see http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/counting.critters/

messages.subject: non-invasive marking of points?
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

We are working in a national park with a =93non-invasive research=94 policy =
in
effect.  This means we cannot mark point count stations with any obvious
signs such as flagging, tree tags, or paint.  An acceptable method to
permanently mark a point is to place a nail in a wooden stake and drive
this in so that it is flush with the ground and then use a metal detector
to relocate this point.  Well, I=92m about to drive a stake into myself!  We=

have over 200 points in this study and it just doesn=92t seem reasonable to
carry a metal detector in the field.  We want these points to be permanent
since this will be part of a long term monitoring study which will include
vegetation sampling.

First, does anyone have experience with or suggestions for non-invasively
marking points?  Second is it necessary to sample the exact location every
time?  We will be using a GPS unit to mark and relocate points which under
average conditions gets us to within 10-20 m of the point.

Thanks so much and happy field days to you all!
Kim Ferree

--

messages.subject: Re: non-invasive marking of points?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kimberley

I have a system which I use for discreet marking of points where the
situation requires. I use a tree which is in the vicinity and is clearly
identifiable- take a photo & write a description & use your GPS to find it
the next time. Then I use a magnetic bearing and measured distance from the
tree to the point location.

When you need to go back to the point it is just a matter of standing out
from the tree and finding the point at the distance and bearing from the
tree. I have no trouble finding a small peg even in thick ground cover this
way and I use this method for relocating individual plants being monitored
often over years.

I use a Leica Disto Classic 3 and a Suunto KB14/360 R. This will certainly
get you standing in the same spot each time.

Cheers

Colin Driscoll

metal detector in the field.  We want these points to be permanent since
this will be part of a long term monitoring study which will include
vegetation sampling.

First, does anyone have experience with or suggestions for non-invasively
marking points?  Second is it necessary to sample the exact location every
time?  We will be using a GPS unit to mark and relocate points which under
average conditions gets us to within 10-20 m of the point.

Thanks so much and happy field days to you all!
Kim Ferree

messages.subject: Re: non-invasive marking of points?
messages.body_plain:
I agree with Colin that relocation isn't too problematic provided you have
good notes.  Laser rangefinders make it easy to record exact distances to
help locate points.  Having a photo of a useful feature near the point
seems an excellent idea.  Apart from the issue of carrying a metal
detector around, you would need to achieve much better accuracy than
10-20m, to be able to find the peg in a reasonable time, so a written
description of the location would be needed anyway.

Accuracy in relocating the point is less important for bird surveys than
for plant surveys, and for most purposes, the nearest 10-20m may be OK.
But a brief written description should allow you to improve this accuracy
appreciably, even if you didn't bother to relocate the point exactly.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: spatial models
messages.body_plain:
hello,

here is chapter 3 (I hope the final one ) of my attempt to make a spatial
model of fallow deer distribution using line transect data (cap 4 of
advanced distance sampling book). To give a framework to the reader  I've
reported below my previous questions.

I order to check if the results were reasonable, I compared them with the
results of CDS using the same LT data.

The CDS yielded  a cluster density of 15.161 per km2 (CV=9.59) and an animal
density of 41.068 (CV=11.3)

The spatial model yielded an average cluster density of 11.1 and an animal
density of  31.6.

This result might be reasonable because probably the dense woods where
fallow deer are less likely to be found are also less likely to be sampled
by the observer, despite we tried to distribute transects at random.

The question now is how to compute a CV value for the spatial model (with a
special regards to cluster density)

Is the problem solved of I have to discuss this result in a purely
qualitative way without making any statistical comparison between the CDS
and "spatial" estimates?

thanks

Stefano

Stefano Focardi

Istituto Nazionale per la Fauna Selvatica
via Ca' Fornacetta, 9
40064 Ozzano dell'Emilia
Italy

tel. ++390516512223
fax ++39051796628
e-mai:l stefano...@infs.it

============= 2 chapter
=============================================================
> > with reference to my previous question dated 29/11/04 I was able to write
a software to apply a methods described in chapter 4 (section 4.3) of the
book Advanced distance sampling by Buckland et al.
> >
> > and that system seems working appropriately in the sense that the model
predicts the distribution of radiocollared fallow deer in the area.
> >
> > However some doubts remain.
> >
> > 1. I've used 4 surveys to estimate local fallow deer density. To do that I
used the ESW estimated by pooling the data of the 4 surveys and the waiting
distance I used all points of the 4 surveys. By instance
> >
> > A------B-----A------------C (translated transect of fig 4.1)
> > x1.....x2...x3...........x4 coordinates
> >
> > I computed  l_i=x2-x1 between A and B, between B  and A (x3-x2) and so on
where A,B,C are detection  points from the first, second,.. survey.
> >
> > I argued that the density obtained is the "average density" of the 4
surveys but I worry whether or I've to divide by 4 (or for some other value)
to obtain it?

Yes, by pooling, you're increased the encounter rate fourfold, so you will
need to divide the density estimate by 4.

> > 2. Fallow deer occurs in clusters. For each point of the grid used to
extrapolate the model, I used the following equations derived by eq. (4.1)
> >
> > D_hat=s_hat/2*mu_hat*l_hat
> >
> > where s_hat is the average cluster size per habitat (we detected no size
bias). Is this correct or there are smarter way to modelise s_hat?

That should be fine.  You could also fit a spatial model for s - see p68
of the advanced distance sampling book.

=====================1 chapter
==========================================================
Stefano, we hope to have the simple count method in Distance within the
next year.  More sophisticated methods, including methods that model
autocorrelation, are a bit further down the line, but should be in
Distance in under 3 years.  Meantime:

> > In wish to perform a spatial distance sampling analysis in order to
> > develop a spatially explicit map for density in a roe deer population of
> > conservation interest. The aim is to identify  high density areas where
> > to adopt "expensive" conservation measures.
> >
> > During the last years a number of classical distance sampling surveys
> > were made through the study area, trying to estimate population size but
> > where the exact location of the animals was also recorded
> >
> > I've studied cap 4 of "Advanced distance sampling" book for spatial
> > line transects method,  but before developing a procedure in SAS to do
> > the job I'd like to be sure about some points which I've not well
> > understood.
> >
> > all OK until eq 4.4 . I've not understood what f((u1....) is.

This is the probability density function of detection locations (u,v),
evaluated at each location that you detected an animal, and the product
taken across the detected animals.

> > section 4.3
> >
> > the GAM has to be fitted to spatial covariates z. I presume that in the
> > most simple case one should use the x coordinates, or both the x and y
> > coordinates?

Yes, in the simplest case, z would probably be x and y.  The x and y
distances would then be proxies for whatever it is that causes variation
in animal density within your survey region.

> > pag 56. is mu_hat  the effective strip width estimated from CDS on the
> > whole study area?

Yes.  We're working on methods to integrate estimation of mu with the
spatial modelling, but we're not there yet.

> > it is not clear to me how to adjust the waiting distance l . I do not
> > understand the difference between D_hat (x,0) and D_hat (xi,0).
> >
> >  I presume that D_hat (xi,0) is the average density estimated by CDS
> > but what I missed what really means  D_hat (xi,0)is the value obtained
> > from eq.
> >
> > (2mu_hat l)^-1

Having fitted the density surface D^(x,y), then D^(x_i,0) is the value of
this function at x=x_i (the x value of detection i) and y=0.  D^(x,0) is
still this function evaluated at y=0, but now with no value substituted in
for x.  Hence the 2-dimensional surface is now a one-dimensional function,
which we integrate between x=x_{i-1} and x=x_i.

> > I imagine that what I'd do is to compute the mean density for the whole
> > study area using the values estimated for each segment and "oblige" the
> > program to set that CDS density and spatial DS density be the same over
> > the whole study area.

That is not what we intend, as the spatial method can give you a more
precise estimate of overall density.  If you rescale it to match the CDS
estimate, you will lose the extra precision.

> > Finally, what can be a good criterion to establish that iteration has
> > converged? Maybe that
> >
> > absolute value (mean of D_hat (xi,0) - CDS density) <0.0001?

It depends on the units you're using to estimate density, but it converges
quickly, so any small value is likely to work well.  One possibility might
be that l'_i in one iteration differs from the previous iteration by less
than 0.0001*l'_i for each i.
